prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Genial poets, pink-faced earnest wits— you have given the world some choice morsels, gobbets of language presented as one presents T-bone steak and Cherries Jubilee. Goodbye, goodbye, I don’t care if I never taste your fine food again, neutral fellows, seers of every side. Tolerance, what crimes are committed in your name. And you, good women, bakers of nicest bread, blood donors. Your crumbs choke me, I would not want a drop of your blood in me, it is pumped by weak hearts, perfect pulses that never falter: irresponsive to nightmare reality. It is my brothers, my sisters, whose blood spurts out and stops forever because you choose to believe it is not your business. Goodbye, goodbye, your poems shut their little mouths, your loaves grow moldy, a gulf has split the ground between us, and you won’t wave, you’re looking another way. We shan’t meet again— unless you leap it, leaving behind you the cherished worms of your dispassion, your pallid ironies, your jovial, murderous, wry-humored balanced judgment, leap over, un- balanced? ... then how our fanatic tears would flow and mingle for joy ...

Here are two polished versions of the text, depending on the specific tone you wish to achieve. Both retain all original meaning, imagery, and structural logic while elevating the eloquence, vocabulary, and flow.

### Option 1: Elevated & Literary (Recommended)
*This version preserves the dramatic intensity and vivid poetic imagery of the original while refining the rhythm, phrasing, and artistic elegance.*

> “Affable poets and earnest, rosy-faced wits—you have offered the world choice morsels of language, presented like fine steaks and Cherries Jubilee. Farewell; I care not if I ever sample your refined offerings again, you neutral bystanders who claim to see every side. What atrocities are committed in the name of tolerance! And to you, virtuous women, bakers of wholesome bread, and charitable blood donors: your crumbs suffocate me. I would not accept a single drop of your blood; it is pumped by faint hearts with steady, unfeeling beats, entirely oblivious to nightmarish reality. It is my brothers and sisters whose blood spills and ceases to flow forever, simply because you choose to believe it is none of your concern. 
> 
> Farewell. Your poems close their lips, your bread gathers mold, and a deep chasm has split the earth between us. Yet you do not wave; you avert your eyes. We shall not meet again—unless you leap across the divide, leaving behind the cherished parasites of your indifference, your pale ironies, and your jovial, lethal, wryly balanced judgment. Should you leap over into our passionate imbalance, how our tears of devotion would flow and mingle in joy.”

---

### Option 2: Formal & Persuasive
*This version adapts the text into a polished, high-level rhetorical statement suitable for a formal essay, speech, or critique.*

> “To the agreeable poets and well-meaning intellectuals: you have provided society with exquisite fragments of language, served like indulgent delicacies. Farewell; I have no desire to consume your refined rhetoric any longer, nor do I align with your neutral stance as observers who claim to see every side. Incalculable harm is committed under the mantle of tolerance. To the well-intentioned moralists and passive benefactors: your quiet virtues are suffocating. Your placid composure remains undisturbed by harrowing realities, while the blood of my brothers and sisters is shed because you choose non-involvement. 
> 
> Farewell. Your art falls silent, your contributions decay, and a vast divide now separates us—one you deliberately ignore. We will not meet again unless you dare to cross this abyss, abandoning your cherished detachment, subtle ironies, and dangerously balanced judgment. Only if you abandon this composure and join us will our passionate tears finally mingle in shared joy.”

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Flow & Cadence:** Reorganized sentence transitions to create a powerful, rhythmic cadence without losing the raw emotion.
* **Refined Vocabulary:** Elevated phrases like "pink-faced earnest wits" to "earnest, rosy-faced wits" / "well-meaning intellectuals," and "cherished worms of your dispassion" to "cherished parasites of your indifference."
* **Clarity of Metaphor:** Maintained the contrast between the passive, "balanced" group and the passionate, suffering group while making the core accusation clearer and more resonant.

Friendly verse-makers and sincere, sharp-witted thinkers have offered humanity exquisite linguistic delicacies, serving their words like high-end steaks and fancy desserts. Farewell to all of you; I have zero desire to savor your refined art ever again, you unbiased observers who try to justify all perspectives. It is appalling how much wickedness is sanctioned under the banner of open-mindedness. 

To the virtuous women who bake fine loaves and donate blood: your leftovers suffocate me, and I refuse to take a single drop of your fluid. It flows from frail organs whose steady, flawless beats remain completely unmoved by terrifying horrors. The life force of my kin erupts and ends permanently, all because you elect to pretend their fate is none of your concern. 

So farewell: your verses close their lips, your baked goods rot away, and a massive abyss now divides us. You refuse to acknowledge me, intentionally turning your gaze in another direction. We will never cross paths again unless you jump across that rift, abandoning your precious apathy, your weak sarcasm, and your friendly yet lethal sense of compromise. Should you abandon your composure and take that wild leap, our passionate, unrestrained tears would merge in pure delight.
outputs.L3:
In times of profound crisis, neutrality is not a virtue; it is a confession of moral failure. The speaker forcefully rejects the figure of the detached artist and the witty intellectual who hide behind aesthetic refinement while the world burns around them. To craft elegant, polished art while remaining indifferent to real-world oppression is an abdication of basic human duty. This calculated neutrality and passive tolerance are far from noble—they function as an anesthetic to the conscience, actively enabling systemic crimes by refusing to confront and name the nightmare realities of the era.

Because of this enabling silence, the speaker refuses to grant absolution to the bystander. Dispassionate and uninvolved individuals cannot claim innocence; they are held directly accountable for the ongoing suffering and loss of life surrounding them. Silence in the face of atrocity is never impartial; it is a tacit endorsement of the oppressor. The bloodshed and injustice of the world rest heavily on the shoulders of those who possess the privilege, voice, and intellect to act, yet choose the comfort of detachment.

Consequently, a deep and irreconcilable divide has formed between the speaker and those who choose to ignore societal violence. This is not a mere difference of artistic style or philosophical opinion, but an unbridgeable moral rupture. There can be no genuine fellowship between those who bear witness to human suffering and those who actively avert their gaze to protect their own peace of mind.

Yet, this divide does not have to be permanent, though the terms for healing it are non-negotiable. Reconciliation can only occur if these neutral individuals abandon their cold dispassion and surrender the illusion of safe equilibrium. To bridge the chasm, they must cast aside calculated moderation and embrace a passionate, unyielding, and fiercely dedicated commitment to the cause of justice. True solidarity demands nothing less than total engagement in the struggle for human dignity.
outputs.L4:
**The Myth of the Quiet Spectator**

There is a insidious violence in the poise of the detached observer. Across centuries of crisis, we have witnessed the rise of a particular archetype: the poet who polishes stanzas of aesthetic distance while the world burns, and the citizen who mistakes their silence for civil restraint. Hiding behind a shield of “balanced tolerance,” these arbiters of moderation view the agonies of human suffering not as a call to action, but as a complex equation to be weighed from a safe distance. They pride themselves on seeing "all sides," treating the cry of the oppressed and the violence of the oppressor as equal components of a grand, tragic tapestry. But this cool, intellectual distance is not wisdom; it is moral cowardice dressed in the robes of philosophy.

We must forcefully reject this bloodless sanctuary. To stand in the middle of a burning house and preach the virtues of temperance is not neutrality—it is complicity. When human dignity is actively stripped away, the insistence on dispassionate moderation functions merely as an endorsement of the status quo. The dispassionate poet who refuses to let their verse burn with outrage, and the quiet citizen who elevates calm above justice, are complicit in the very horrors they claim to lament. Their neutrality does not protect them from the moral wreckage of their era; it simply ensures that their legacy will be written in the ink of indifference.

It is time to challenge these spectators to descend from their sanctimonious heights. To truly honor the human condition, one must abandon the illusion of the objective bystander. The divide between the safe observer and the suffering victim cannot be bridged by mere intellectual sympathy or passive goodwill. It requires a radical rupture of one's own comfort. It demands that the poet trade immaculate form for raw, uncompromising truth, and that the citizen swap the ease of non-involvement for the burden of public advocacy. 

Ultimately, emotional reconciliation and genuine peace cannot be cultivated in the cold soil of passivity. They require the heat of fervent solidarity. True empathy is not a quiet feeling to be cultivated in isolation; it is an active, living commitment to step into the crucible of another’s pain. Only when we relinquish the armor of comfortable neutrality and plunge into the mess of active moral engagement can we begin to heal the fractures of our shared world. Humanity does not need more balanced observers; it demands passionate witnesses who understand that to care is, fundamentally, to take a side.

The late afternoon sun cast a honeyed glow over the hillside orchard, where the branches bowed heavy under the weight of the season’s richest bounty. It was the evening of the annual summer festival, an occasion marked by music, effortless camaraderie, and shared gratitude. At the center of the festivities stood Arthur, a man whose **genial** hospitality had drawn the entire community together. With a booming laugh, a warm handshake for every guest, and an easygoing spirit, he ensured that no stranger remained isolated for long.

Tables stretched across the lawn, but the true stars of the evening hung in thick, glossy clusters from the trees. Deep crimson and perfectly plump, the ripe **cherries** caught the fading light like polished rubies. Guests wandered through the rows, filling wicker baskets and enjoying the fruit’s sweet, sun-warmed juice. 

As twilight deepened and string lights flickered to life overhead, Arthur gathered the crowd around a grand outdoor stove for the evening's main event. With the theatrical flourish of a seasoned host, he poured warm brandy into a sizzling pan of simmered fruit and set it alight. A brilliant flash of blue flame illuminated the smiling faces of the onlookers, igniting a chorus of cheers. 

Serving spoonfuls of the warm, rich Cherries **Jubilee** over mounds of cold vanilla ice cream, Arthur raised a glass to the crowd. It was more than just a dessert; it was a celebration of friendship, hard work, and the sweet abundance of summer—a true **jubilee** that would be remembered long after the last lights faded.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fiery, poetic monologue condemning people who remain neutral and moderate during times of atrocity.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker stands before a crowd, eyes blazing, voice low and trembling with an unrestrained, terrifying heat. As they speak, the voice rises, cutting through the air like a blade.)*

Look at you. Standing in the ashes with unsoiled shoes. 

You call it *wisdom*, don’t you? You call it *prudence*. You sit in the middle of a burning sanctuary, sipping your lukewarm tea, weighing the merits of the flame against the pleas of the burning flesh, and you dare to call yourself *civilized*!

Do not speak to me of your balance! Do not dare utter the phrase "both sides" while the earth beneath your feet drinks the warm, violent blood of the innocent! You, the quiet ones. You, the measured ones. You who cultivate a spineless gray in a world that is screaming in blinding red and absolute black.

Tell me—what is the middle ground between the boot and the neck? What is the polite compromise between the butcher and the lamb? Will you negotiate a surrender where only half the bones are crushed? Will you ask the tyrant to strike with a softer iron, so as not to disturb your delicate sensibilities?

You think your hands are clean because you never pulled the trigger. You think your hands are clean because you held them up in surrender to the storm! But I see the stains on you. I see the phantom blood dripping from your polished sleeves. When you remain neutral in the presence of atrocity, you do not stand above the fray—you lie beneath it, acting as the carpet for the oppressor to walk upon!

Silence is not a sanctuary. Silence is an endorsement. 

The murderer does not fear the enemy who fights back half as much as he loves the spectator who turns away. Your moderation is his license. Your hesitation is his shield. You hand him the axe, and then you weep over the wood, pretending you had no part in the felling of the forest!

Oh, Dante knew your names! He knew the lukewarm souls who were neither faithful nor rebellious, but existed only for themselves. Even Hell refused you, lest the damned feel a moment of superiority over creatures so thoroughly hollow! 

The world is on fire! Children are crying out from the rubble of your precious, fragile order, and you stand there measuring the wind! You fear the heat of commitment, so you freeze in your cowardice. You fear being wrong, so you forfeit the right to ever be good!

Hear me, you fence-sitters, you polite orchestrators of apathy: history will not remember your carefully drafted disclaimers. The fire will not respect your neutrality. When the dust settles and the ledgers of this dark age are finally read, the monsters will be condemned for their cruelty—but you… *you* will be remembered for the permission you gave them.

So keep your coward’s peace. Keep your bloodless hands. But do not call yourselves innocent. You are the grease on the wheels of catastrophe. 

Choose! Choose now, before the fire chooses for you, you miserable, hollow spectators of the end!
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic prose poem in the style of mid-20th-century political poetry that rejects polite, dispassionate intellectuals and moderate 'good citizens,' using vivid imagery of blood, bread, and a widening gulf.
counterfactuals.output:
Curse your balanced syntax, your quiet studies, your neat symposia where horror is weighed on silver scales. We have grown sick of the good citizen—that well-mannered neighbor who washes his hands before the morning execution, provided the lawn remains manicured and the ledger stays in the black. You, the dispassionate thinkers, sit high above the soot of the foundries, refining your delicate distinctions while the sky roars with iron. You offer us a footnote where we demanded a weapon; you preach patience to a room full of hemorrhaging men. 

Do you truly believe history will honor your neutrality? Look down from your balconies. The bread in our hands is heavy, coarse, and sour with sweat—it was not baked with your abstract theories, but torn from the teeth of a bitter season by fingers split to the bone. And the blood—the blood is not a literary trope to be discussed over sherry. It is hot, thick, and heavy with iron; it runs down the granite steps of your university libraries, soaking into the hems of your trousers whether you step carefully over the puddle or pretend it is only rain. You cannot sanitize the butcher’s apron with proper grammar.

The earth is tearing open beneath your velvet armchairs. Between your quiet, reasonable dining rooms and the howling mass of the betrayed, a gulf widens—black, jagged, and absolute. There is no middle ground on a collapsing bridge. There is no polite compromise between the boot and the throat. Every hour you spend debating the decorum of our rage, the chasm grows deeper, filling with the quiet cowardice of the moderate and the ash of burned harvest fields.

Keep your sanitized pity. Keep your clean hands and your bloodless consensus. We reject your temperate, well-dressed ruin. Leave us the raw bread, the cold mud, and the terrible red tide—for history will not ask how gracefully you articulated the catastrophe, but which side of the rift you stood on when the world broke in two.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a radical artist giving a bitter farewell speech to their former circle of witty, moderate poet friends who refuse to take a side in a moral crisis.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker stands at the head of the crowded parlor table, holding a glass of cheap wine. The ambient laughter of the salon dies down, replaced by a tense, expectant silence. The speaker’s coat is splattered with paint and street dust; the audience wears tailored wool and velvet.)*

Raise your glasses, my brilliant friends. Go on, lift them up. Let’s have one last toast to the sharpest wits in the city, the masters of the clever turn-of-phrase, the high priests of *moderation*.

How I envy you all. Truly. What a magnificent luxury it must be to possess a mind so agile, so exquisitely refined, that it can find a middle ground between the boot and the neck. 

Look at you. You sit here in the warm glow of your candlelight, sipping vintage port, while the streets outside are burning. A monstrous brutality is unfolding at our very doorsteps—people are being crushed, erased, bled dry—and what do you do? You write sonnets about the "tragic complexity of it all." You draft clever little epigrams mourning the loss of *decorum*. 

You call your silence "nuance." You call your hesitation "intellectual rigor." But let’s drop the metaphors for once, shall we? It isn’t nuance. It’s cowardice. It’s the comfortable apathy of men and women who know that no matter who wins this war, your trust funds and tenured seats will remain intact. You have weaponized irony just to shield yourselves from the indignity of having a spine.

When I first met you, I thought your wit was a razor meant to cut through the lies of this world. Now I see it’s just a butter knife, dull and safe, used to spread your respectable little compromises. You’re terrified of taking a side because taking a side means risking something. It means losing the admiration of the very monsters who buy your books. You’d rather be thought clever by tyrants than be hated for standing with the damned.

Art is not a parlor trick to make your privilege taste better. It isn't a polite evening soundtrack for the collapse of civilization. Art is a hammer! It is a flare shot into the dark! It is supposed to burn the hands of anyone who tries to tame it. But you’ve turned your ink into perfume, choking out the stench of blood with sweet, bloodless metaphors.

So, keep your salon. Keep your polite debates and your delicate, balanced rhyming couplets. When the history of this atrocity is written, your names won't be recorded as the great thinkers of our age. You will be a footnote—a chorus of well-dressed cowards who hummed in harmony while the world burned around them.

I am done trying to shake you awake. I’m leaving this room, and I’m taking my fire with me. 

Enjoy your wine, ladies and gentlemen. I hope it doesn't taste too much of ash.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: A prose poem railing against tolerance and balanced judgment.
counterfactuals.output:
Curse the tepid bath, the grey sludge of the middle distance, the lukewarm soup of our collective surrender. We are drowning in a swamp of polite nods, dying of a slow, bloodless moderation that calls itself maturity. Look at them—the priests of the middle ground, hovering over life’s agony with their brass scales and surgical gloves, frantically measuring out equal portions of venom and honey, as if the universe were a ledger to be balanced by cowards.

Balanced judgment is a paralysis of the heart, a bloodless math applied to a world on fire. It is the arrogance of holding a wooden ruler up to a hurricane, the sheer, insult-to-gods stupidity of demanding to hear "both sides" of a burning house—the side of the timber and the side of the flame. To weigh every horror against its context until the horror vanishes into anemic reasoning is not wisdom; it is the art of feeling nothing while pretending to understand everything. It is the quiet, methodical strangulation of impulse.

And tolerance—this flabby, worshiped idol! We have mistaken the inability to feel for the grace to accept. Tolerance is the slop we feed to our teeth so they forget how to bite. It is the weed choking the rose, while the gardener stands by with his arms folded, smiling benignly at the chaos, calling his laziness a virtue. To tolerate everything is to love nothing. It is to smile at the blade as it slides between your ribs because, after all, the steel has its own valid point of view.

Give me the razor edge. Give me the holy violence of an absolute. Give me the man who screams *No* until his throat splits, or *Yes* until the stars shake, but spare me the man who smiles, sighs, and sits on the fence until the wood rots beneath him. The cosmic forge was not lit with a polite consensus; it was smashed into being by collision, by fury, by unyielding light tearing through unyielding dark. 

Shatter the scales. Melt the brass. Better to plunge headlong into a magnificent, catastrophic error than to rot away in the air-conditioned purgatory of a perfectly balanced life. Let the world be sharp again, or let it not be at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intense literary passage contrasting the comfortable, bloodless lives of passive bystanders with the active suffering of those on the frontlines, ending with a plea for them to abandon their dispassion and join the fanatic struggle.
counterfactuals.output:
You dwell in the quiet pale of the unblemished, cradled by the soft, suffocating upholstery of your own restraint. Yours is a world measured in tepid tea, in polite murmurs, in the neat, bloodless geometry of folded linen and double-pane glass that keeps the howling night at bay. You watch the storm through a frame, sipping your spirits, your hands smooth and pale as unturned soil, your pulse a slow, rhythmic clock ticking toward a seamless, forgotten grave. You take pride in your balance, your temperance, your immaculate distance. You call it wisdom; you call it peace. But it is not peace—it is only the quiet decay of those who have agreed to die by inches so long as the dying is clean.

Out here, on the razor’s edge of existence, there is no room for the luxury of your dispassion. Here, the earth is not a floor but a gullet, slick with mud and the hot, iron tang of torn flesh. Out here, life is not weighed in gentle arguments, but wrenched from the throat in jagged, desperate gasps. We stand drenched in the ruin of the world, our fingers caked in soot and grease, our muscles screaming beneath the terrible, sublime weight of a cause that demands everything and returns only scars. We bleed not in metaphor, but in crimson torrents that stain the dirt beneath our knees. Every breath we draw is an agony; every step forward is taken through the shattered bones of our former selves. We are scorched, we are broken, we are utterly consumed—and yet, in this terrible fire, we are blindingly, brutally alive.

How dare you offer us your pity from the safety of your pristine shadow? How dare you judge the madness of the drowning from the dry comfort of the shore? Your neutrality is not a virtue; it is a rot. It is the cowardice of the unborn, the sterile silence of those who would rather be nothing at all than risk the magnificent, ruinous cost of feeling.

Cast off the velvet shroud! Smash the glass that shields your delicate skin from the cinder and the blade! Step out of the parlor and into the forge. Strip away your precious, bloodless sanity and drown it in the mud alongside us. Let your clean hands be ruined; let your smooth skin be carved by the truth of the fight. Do not watch us burn from afar—leap into the pyre! For it is infinitely better to be consumed by the incandescent fury of a holy struggle, to scream until the lungs tear and the heart explodes, than to live a thousand years as a quiet, porcelain ghost, watching the world bleed out from behind a closed window. Join us in the dirt, or admit that you were never alive to begin with.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
